cells.tense: What you gave is out in the open now, and you are here with the pen in hand.
cells.ask: Name one thing you finished this month and the person who watched you do it, in one plain sentence to them, without explaining what it cost. Then leave it there.
cells.core: The day a thing gets finished in front of people, and the effort is seen, and you let it count as done — that day is ordinary for you. No inflating it, no running it down to stay modest. You've set down what took months, you know what you traded for it, and you're not holding it up like a bill waiting to be paid. Finishing sits steady on you rather than turning compulsive. You look after what you've built without gripping it so hard it can't breathe, and that work isn't wearing you down. What you hand somebody stays whole after it leaves your hands, and people can see the shape of what you gave up to make it.
cells.sheetLine: Done, seen, and held loosely — all three at once.
cells.verb: letting what you gave be seen and counted
cells.place: the threshold where a finished thing is still warm in your hands

cells.tense: You are pushing toward an acknowledgment that hasn't arrived and won't run on your schedule.
cells.ask: Find one thing you did well this week that nobody mentioned, write down what you actually did, then close the file and don't rework it.
cells.core: The easy shape is simple: a thing gets finished, you let it go, and you move to the next one without needing the verdict first. That letting go is what's slipping. The effort is real and the finishing is real, but you keep living in the aftermath instead of the work — every completed piece becomes a case to argue, and each person who might weigh in becomes a vote to secure. Bracing for a reaction that hasn't come spends the ease that would let you release the thing and start the next. Your eye for what matters is sharp and getting sharper. It just isn't pointed at the table in front of you.
cells.sheetLine: You're asking for the thanks before the work is done.
cells.verb: letting what you gave be seen and counted
cells.place: the threshold where a finished thing is still warm in your hands

cells.tense: You closed the door on something you handed over, and you are still in the hallway.
cells.ask: Take one thing you finished and did not announce, and tell one person it happened this week. Not asking for praise — just stating it.
cells.core: When this runs right, a finished thing gets set down and the next one starts. That setting down is the missing piece. You finish reliably; the strength is there and it holds, and you carry what you carry without complaint. But when something ends, it stays in the hallway with you instead of going out where it could be seen, so nothing closes into a door you can walk through. No one hands you a verdict because you haven't handed the thing over. The persistence is doing its job, holding steady under weight. It's aimed at keeping the thing close rather than at putting it down and letting it stand where the light falls.
cells.sheetLine: You did the work. You stopped expecting anyone to know.
cells.verb: letting what you gave be seen and counted
cells.place: the threshold where a finished thing is still warm in your hands

cells.tense: You are already shaping what gets honored around you, but you don't call it that.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you did that someone else got thanked for, and tell them you were part of it. State it once, plainly, no hedging.
cells.core: The strong shape is someone who finishes a thing in public and lets the credit land where it lands. You do that — quietly deciding which effort gets praised, what goes unremarked, how you talk about your own finished work. What doesn't happen is naming it. You describe the recognition you get as if it arrived on its own from somewhere, a verdict from outside, when you're the one shaping what counts as worth honoring in your circles. Finishing well and looking after what's around you both get done. The part that isn't is the part where you say the shaping is yours. The work stands either way. Your hand in it goes unnamed.
cells.sheetLine: You shape what gets honored. You haven't said so.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has actually gone unrecognized by anyone, and it cannot; my draft reads their history into the card's shape. A reader could reasonably say the recognition already happened and they simply stopped keeping it — that this is memory, not current standing. The ask survives either way: a report to one person is useful whether the problem is that no one appreciated it or that they will not believe anyone did. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about being unseen; I'll aim it at the seeing they aren't doing.
